To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) scores of knowledge and shared decision making (SDM) were similar 1 year and 1 month after breast cancer surgical treatment decision; (2) the site offering formal decision support services had significantly higher knowledge scores at 1 year after decision and significantly higher SDM Process scores both 1 year and at 1 month after decision; and (3) a substantial percentage of patients had increases or decreases in their scores over time.
knowledge and decision making scores did not differ between 1 and 12 months after the surgery decision, and the site using formal decision aids had higher scores.
knowledge scores and SDM Process measures are stable over a 12 month period, and that the use of decision support is associated with higher scores.

the impact of timing of the assessment on measurement of decision quality and shared decision making in breast cancer patients.
the impact that the timing of measurement has on the scores of decision quality and shared decision-making measures.
the measurement of decision making in patients with breast cancer, and the impact of decision support interventions on this process.

the impact on decision quality and SDM process scores of a formal decision support program was not significantly different at either 1 month or 1 year after treatment.
the decision-making scores were not different over time, but the impact of the timing of measurement on scores is complex.
there is no evidence to support the idea that timing has an impact on measurement of decision quality or shared decision-making.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the impact of timing on shared decision making is not as important as the quality of the decision support provided.
there is no significant difference between the two time points, but the 1-month time point is more sensitive to change.
it is not necessary to measure knowledge and decision making shortly after the decision is made, and it is not necessary for patients to have a high knowledge score to make a good decision.

the timing of measurement of decision quality and SDM may have an impact on the scores.
there is a lot of variation in scores over time, which should be taken into account in study designs.
